prompt: Develop a preliminary solar-water-heating plan for a residential building with 40 residents. Present exactly five workflow steps. Cover demand assessment, key components and connections, seasonal/backup operation, installation and maintenance risks, and performance checks. Roof area, local climate, water-use measurements and energy prices are unknown. Identify missing information and how it affects choices instead of inventing exact sizes, savings or costs. Keep the plan under 550 words.
answer:
1. **Assess hot-water demand and site conditions.** Use 40 residents as the occupancy baseline, then measure daily hot-water use, peak draw periods, delivery temperatures and cold-water inlet temperatures. Confirm occupancy patterns and existing heating equipment. Obtain usable roof area, shading, orientation, structural capacity, local solar radiation, temperatures and freeze exposure. These inputs determine feasible collector capacity, storage volume and solar contribution; occupancy alone cannot establish sizes.

2. **Select components and map connections.** Compare flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors against climate, roof constraints and service availability. Plan insulated storage, circulation equipment, controls, expansion vessels, pressure/temperature relief, isolation valves and a thermostatic mixing valve for safe delivery. A typical arrangement is **collectors → heat-transfer loop → storage heat exchanger; potable cold water → solar storage → backup heater → mixing valve → building distribution**. Select direct, indirect antifreeze or drainback circulation only after confirming freeze risk, water quality and applicable codes. Account for distribution and recirculation heat losses.

3. **Define seasonal and backup operation.** Use differential-temperature controls to collect heat when collectors are hotter than storage. Provide backup heating capable of meeting the required load during low sunshine, peak demand or solar-system outages. Choose the backup fuel and control strategy after obtaining existing equipment details, electrical capacity and energy tariffs. Establish climate-appropriate freeze protection and a summer overheating strategy, including low-occupancy conditions. Maintain hygienic storage and distribution temperatures under local requirements, with scald protection at delivery.

4. **Review installation and maintenance risks.** Require structural assessment, approved roof anchoring, waterproof penetrations, wind/snow-load checks and safe maintenance access. Address hot surfaces, working at height, leaks, corrosion, scaling, electrical safety and compatibility between heat-transfer fluids and potable-water protection requirements. Route relief discharges safely and provide accessible isolation and drainage. Set a maintenance schedule for collector inspection, insulation, pumps, valves, sensors, fluid condition and any sacrificial anodes. Water chemistry and local service capability affect equipment selection and maintenance frequency.

5. **Verify performance before committing and after commissioning.** Model feasible options using measured demand, local weather, actual roof constraints and distribution losses. Compare annual useful solar heat, backup energy, overheating risk and lifecycle cost; obtain installed quotations and energy prices before estimating savings or payback. At commissioning, verify flow, sensor readings, controls, leak tightness, mixing temperatures and safety devices. Meter hot-water consumption, useful solar heat and backup energy, then compare weather- and occupancy-adjusted results with predictions across seasons. Investigate shortfalls before expanding or resizing the system.
